author: high
claim: Direct proof of the forward implication: bipartite implies no odd cycle (solved).
evidence: Assume V(G)=A∪B is a bipartition. Every edge traversal changes from A to B or from B to A. Hence after an odd number of traversals one lies in the class opposite the starting class. Traversing a cycle returns to its starting vertex, which lies in its original class; since A and B are disjoint, the number of traversed edges cannot be odd. Thus every cycle has even length.

links.attempt_summary: Cycle traversal alternates the two vertex classes.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph in the theorem
glossary.A: the first part of a bipartition of V(G)
glossary.B: the second part of a bipartition of V(G)
glossary.H: an arbitrary connected component of G
glossary.r: the chosen root vertex of T
glossary.u: one endpoint of an arbitrary edge of H
glossary.v: the other endpoint of that edge
glossary.w: the last common vertex on the root-to-u and root-to-v paths in T
glossary.P: the unique path in T from u to v
glossary.d_T(r,x): the number of edges in the unique path in T from r to x

author: high
claim: Direct proof of the reverse implication: no odd cycle implies bipartite (solved).
evidence: Assume G has no odd cycle. In each connected component H choose a rooted spanning tree T with root r, and divide the vertices according to the parity of d_T(r,x). If an edge uv had endpoints at depths of the same parity, let w be the last common vertex on the root-to-u and root-to-v tree paths. The unique u-v tree path P has length d_T(r,u)+d_T(r,v)-2d_T(r,w), which is even. A loop would itself be a one-edge odd cycle, so u and v are distinct; therefore P has positive even length and uv is not its sole tree edge. Adding uv to P yields a simple cycle of odd length, contradiction. Thus every edge crosses the two parity classes, giving a bipartition componentwise and hence globally.
